overview.text: Chemical concentration describes how much of a chosen component—often a dissolved substance called a solute—is present relative to a specified amount of a mixture or solution. It helps chemists compare solution compositions and calculate amounts used in chemical reactions. Concentration can be described qualitatively as dilute or concentrated, or quantitatively using units with different denominators. Molarity (M) is moles of solute per liter of the entire solution; molality (m) is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Because solution volume can change with temperature, molarity may change as temperature changes, while molality, based on mass, does not. The denominator is the key distinction between these two units.

key_facts.text: Concentration expresses the relative amount of a component in a specified amount of solvent or solution.
Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution; its symbol is capital M.
Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent; its symbol is lowercase m.
Molarity can vary with temperature because solution volume changes; molality does not, since it uses mass.
Molarity can be used to calculate quantities in chemical reactions and solution calculations.
